inference_aids.art_brief: Hamrar baðstofa after supper, mid-November 1874, dark outside. Ink and watercolour. Hallur, still the stranger to most listeners, chants with eyes half closed, fully clothed in worn wool; do not label his identity. Þórunn rises from her wooden spinning wheel as she recognises him. Guðrún has paused knitting; the household sits along the beds, listening. One fish-oil lamp is lit. Siggi holds afi’s Edda; afi sits listening and retains ownership of the book. Show Bjarni, Ásta, Óli, Helga, Manga and Snati consistently with the character bible. Open wooden askur bowls from supper may sit beside the beds, empty or with a little porridge. No lettering.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: „Ég er gestur,“ segir maðurinn. „Ég er ekki gestur,“ segir Bjarni.
„Gestur í snjónum kemur inn,“ segir Guðrún.
„Við köllum hann Gest,“ segir Óli. Gestur er nafn líka.
words_with_history.note_en: Gestur means a guest or stranger and is also an Icelandic personal name. Óli turns the stranger’s evasive answer into the nickname Gestur. Gest is its accusative: the object form after kalla in „Við köllum hann Gest.“ The guest’s „we“ playfully includes the whole household.

pronunciation_note.rule: Preaspiration: pp, tt, kk are said with a puff of h before them (hp, ht, hk): ekki, skotthúfa, rétt

notes: Frozen story: all 97 segment texts, IDs, paragraph starts, speakers, section titles and ordering are preserved verbatim. Apparatus, popups, delta and continuity are rebuilt fresh; no withdrawn exercises or glosses are retained. Draft status does not claim human review.

Learner-load ledger: 28 planned new single lexemes, no extra lexical budget or productive chunks. grammar.title: ég er · við erum · við köllum
grammar.rule: Ég er gestur. · Þú ert forvitin. · Við erum öll gestir.
grammar.note_en:
A person in grammar tells us who speaks or is addressed: first person is the speaker (ég, “I”; við, “we”), second person is the addressee (þú, “you”, one person; þið, “you”, more than one), and third person is someone or something being spoken about (hann, “he”). Singular means one; plural means more than one. The present is the verb form used here for what happens or is true now. The chapter’s opening contrast Ég er gestur … þú ert bóndi (s012) means “I am a guest … you are a farmer.” Þú ert forvitin (s033) means “You are curious”; Við erum öll gestir (s036), “We are all guests.”

Vera means “be”. Its forms change with the subject, the person or thing the sentence is about: ég er, “I am”; þú ert, “you are”; hann er, “he is”; við erum, “we are”; þið eruð, “you all are”; þau eru, “they are”. These are irregular forms: learn the pairs instead of deriving them from one stem. The third-person plural is eru (“they are”), familiar from Kafli 3: Allir eru hér (s027), “Everyone is here”. Allir, “everyone”, is plural in Icelandic, so its verb is plural too.

Hafa means “have”: ég hef, “I have”; þú hefur, “you have”; hann hefur, “he has”; við höfum, “we have”; þið hafið, “you all have”. Ég hef nafn … þú hefur nafn líka (s014) means “I have a name … you have a name too.” Í höllinni hefur hann annað nafn (s050) means “In the hall he has another name.” Hafið þið graut? (s066) means “Do you children have porridge?”; við höfum graut (s067), “we have porridge”. The question puts the verb before the subject; this is shown in the story, without practising a general word-order rule here. The third-person plural is hafa, the same as the dictionary form: allir hafa ask (s063), “everyone has a bowl”.

With kalla (“call”), use kalla for ég, kallar for þú (the same ending as hann kallar), köllum for við and kallið for þið. Óli! Þú kallar hann Gest (s059) means “Óli! You call him Gest.” Ég kalla ykkur forvitin börn (s041) means “I call you curious children”; Við köllum hann Gest (s040), “We call him Gest”; Þið kallið mig Gest (s041), “You call me Gest”. For the ordinary -ar class, remove the final -a of the infinitive, the dictionary form, to find the stem kall-. Add -a for ég, -ar for þú and hann, and -ið for þið. Before the first-person plural ending -um, a changes to ö: kall- + -um gives köllum. This sound change is u-umlaut, familiar from barn → börn (“child → children”). The exercises contrast ég er with við erum, and ég kalla with við köllum. Strong verbs and verbs with an -ir present in the first and second persons come in Kafli 8; this chapter does not extend their paradigms.

A case marks a word’s job in the sentence. The nominative (nf.) is used for the subject; the accusative (þf.) is used for the objects shown here. Ég (“I”) becomes mig (“me”) as the object: Þið kallið mig Gest means “You call me Gest”. Þið (“you”, plural subject) becomes ykkur (“you”, plural object): ég kalla ykkur forvitin börn means “I call you curious children”. The empty cells in the table mean that the corresponding object form has not appeared in this chapter, not that Icelandic has no form there. These are accusative objects; dative objects wait until Kafli 9.

Some expressions are shown as supported chunks, not rules to practise yet. Bærinn minn (s037) is “my farm”; minn agrees with masculine bærinn. Allir (s027) means “everyone”, the household; öll in við erum öll gestir means “all of us”, a mixed group. They will receive fuller treatment later.  Ertu is written as one word: ertu = ert þú, “are you”. This is a clitic: a short, unstressed form of a word attaches to its neighbour. Hvaðan ertu? (s029) means “Where are you from?” Learn the joined form on sight here, without drilling the attachment rule. Hvað ertu að gera? (s069), “What are you doing?”, and Ég er að borða (s070), “I am eating”, show vera að + infinitive. Learn these as whole expressions for an activity in progress; að here is not the preposition meaning “towards”. Ég heiti Gangleri (s048) means “My name is Gangleri”: heiti is a naming formula here, not a new productive first-person paradigm. Komdu inn! (s021), “Come in!”, is likewise a supported invitation, not an imperative paradigm.

Heima answers hvar?, “where?”: hvar ert þú heima? (s084), “where is your home?”; Í kvöld er ég heima hér (s085), “Tonight I am at home here”. Heim answers hvert?, “where to?”: koma heim (s003), “come home”, and hann fer ekki heim um veturinn (s082), “he does not go home during the winter”. Hvaðan? asks “where from?”; úr snjónum (s030) means “out of the snow”. Úr takes the dative: snjó-num is the definite dative form, “the snow”. Contrast that source with the destination í baðstofuna (s024), “into the communal room”.

Með has two uses here. Siggi fer með honum (s008) means “Siggi goes with him”, Bjarni: accompaniment with the dative honum. Guðrún fer með gestinn (s024) means “Guðrún takes the guest along”, and Guðrún kemur með annan ask (s065) means “Guðrún brings another bowl”: taking or bringing along uses the accusative gestinn or annan ask. These are encountered expressions; their contrast is not drilled until later.

Finally, Gestur is both the common noun “guest” and a real Icelandic male name. The household gives the unnamed man the nickname Gestur, “Guest”. In Við köllum hann Gest, Gest is the accusative of that name, not a different person. Hallur is the man’s real name; Hall in Bjarni skoðar Hall (s080) is its accusative. The pun lets the household give him a name before it knows who he is.
